name: Fist to Five
use_case: People leave a meeting apparently in agreement, yet some were fully behind the change, others merely tolerated it and a few had doubts they never voiced, so it is quietly not carried out. To see this while still in the room, everyone shows at the same moment a closed fist or one to five fingers for how strongly they support it, and those showing low numbers say what would have to change for them.
strengths: takes a minute or two and needs nothing but hands, or a chat or poll in a video call
everyone answers at the same moment, so nobody can wait to see what the boss or the majority shows
the graded scale separates 'I can live with it' from real enthusiasm, which a yes/no show of hands hides
low readings are an invitation to speak, so reservations are heard before the plan is settled rather than in the corridor afterwards
can be repeated after the plan is amended, which shows whether the change actually won people over
weaknesses: the reading is public, so in a group with low trust or a strong hierarchy people may show what they think is expected
the meaning of each number and the threshold for going ahead must be agreed beforehand, or the same hand means different things to different people
it only gauges support; who decides, and what happens after a fist, still has to be settled by the group's own decision rule
if every fist simply stops the plan, a single person gets an informal veto
too blunt for sensitive or contested matters, where an anonymous poll or a structured objection round serves better
use_cases: Things seem agreed when the meeting ends, then people drag their feet and admit they had doubts all along; I want a quick way, still in the meeting, to see how much support it really has and who is only tolerating it.
When my team says yes to a change, I can never tell who is truly for it and who just does not want a fuss; I would like everyone to show quickly and at the same time how much they support it.

At the staff meeting the teachers seemed to accept the new rule on mobile phones, yet in the following weeks hardly anyone enforces it; next time the head wants to see on the spot how many really stand behind it before it counts as agreed.

The volunteers of our association agree at the meeting to run the summer fair a new way, but when the day comes only a handful help; next time the organisers want to see first who is really keen and who is only putting up with the idea.

In our working group silence counts as agreement; the chair wants a one-minute check of how much backing the draft really has, so that the hesitant members' reservations come out before the item is closed.

The class agreed on a plan for the school trip, but afterwards several pupils complained they had only gone along with it because their friends did; the teacher wants every pupil to show at the same moment how much they support it.
